prompt.context: A major producer of juice is in the business of processing and packaging fruit juice for retail outlets. Traditionally, the producer has packaged the juice in 18-ounce carton containers. Recently, in response to demand from the market, the producer purchased a machine that packages the juice in plastic gallons (36 ounces). Over the next couple of years, sales continued to grow on average of 20% per year. Yet, as sales continued to increase, profits steadily decreased.
prompt.question: The owner cannot understand why profits are declining despite growing sales. He hires you to help out. Why are profits declining, and what should the owner do?

clarifying_info.q: How much does the producer charge for the 18 oz. carton?
clarifying_info.a: $2.00 per container (originally); later raised to $2.50 after the new machine was purchased.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the producer charge for the 36 oz. plastic gallons?
clarifying_info.a: Originally planned at $3.50 per gallon; later raised to $4.00 after a across-the-board $0.50 price increase to account for new equipment.

clarifying_info.q: Does it cost the same to package juice in cartons as in gallons?
clarifying_info.a: No. Plastic is more expensive than paper cartons, and more experienced (higher-cost) labor is needed to operate the new machine.
All factory costs are added together and divided by the number of units produced — a simple per-unit average across both product types.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of sales are gallons versus cartons?
clarifying_info.a: Plastic gallons have comprised 60% of sales as overall volume grows; the owner has been pleased about that trend.

framework: Use the profitability framework: Revenue - Costs = Profit
Revenue side: sales are growing 20%/year, so revenue is not the root problem — investigate pricing per SKU
Cost side: examine direct costs (packaging material, labor) and overhead allocation method by product type
Cost allocation: determine whether each product line bears its fair share of costs
Pricing: assess whether prices reflect true cost-to-serve for each SKU on a per-ounce basis

questions.prompt: On the revenue side, is pricing appropriate for each container type?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that the gallon at $4.00 offers juice at $0.111/oz while the carton at $2.50 offers juice at $0.139/oz — the larger container is cheaper per ounce even though it costs more to produce. The $0.50 across-the-board price increase does not compensate for the higher incremental costs of the plastic gallon line.

math.setup: Compare price per ounce: 18 oz carton at $2.50 vs 36 oz gallon at $4.00
steps: Gallons are priced ~20% cheaper per ounce despite higher production costs
math.answer: Gallons are under-priced on a per-ounce basis relative to cartons

questions.prompt: On the cost side, how does the overhead allocation method distort profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that averaging all factory costs across all units means cartons effectively subsidize gallon production costs. As gallon share rises (now 60% of volume), the misallocation worsens and total profit falls even as revenue grows.

math.setup: Illustrative blended cost scenario: if gallon-specific costs (material + labor premium) are spread equally across both SKUs, the gallon's true margin is negative while the carton's stated margin is artificially depressed
steps: Higher plastic and labor costs for gallons are pooled with carton costs and divided by total units
Result: gallons appear cheaper to produce per unit than they truly are; cartons appear more expensive than they truly are
More gallon sales → more actual cost incurred → blended average rises → profits erode
math.answer: Cost misallocation causes stated gallon margins to be overstated; as gallon share grows the profit drain accelerates

brainstorming.prompt: What additional costs might the juice producer have failed to account for when launching the plastic gallon line?

categories.name: Direct Material Costs
ideas: Plastic gallon containers cost more than paper cartons
Caps/seals for plastic gallons are an added component
Larger containers require more raw juice per unit if fill tolerances differ

categories.name: Labor Costs
ideas: More experienced (higher-paid) operators needed for the new machine
Training costs for staff on the new equipment
Higher quality-control labor if plastic line has more defects

categories.name: Equipment & Depreciation
ideas: Depreciation of the new plastic-gallon machine
Maintenance and repair costs specific to the new machine
Utilities (power, water) consumed by the new machine

categories.name: Overhead Allocation
ideas: Factory floor space occupied by the new machine
Warehouse space for larger gallon units
Inventory carrying costs (gallons take more space per oz)

categories.name: Logistics & Distribution
ideas: Gallons weigh more, raising shipping costs per oz
Return/spoilage rates if gallons have shorter shelf life once opened

recommendation: Conduct a thorough activity-based costing (ABC) analysis to isolate the direct and overhead costs attributable to each product line (cartons vs. gallons)
Re-price the plastic gallon line to reflect its true cost structure — the current per-ounce price of gallons must be higher, not lower, than cartons given the higher production cost
risks: Re-pricing gallons upward may reduce the volume advantage the owner values, requiring careful elasticity analysis
Customers accustomed to the gallon's lower per-ounce price may switch to competitor brands if the price gap narrows
next_steps: Implement ABC costing system to track costs by SKU
Set gallon price to achieve at least the same per-ounce margin as cartons
Monitor volume mix and total profit monthly to verify the fix is working
Evaluate whether the gallon line is strategically worth maintaining at a correct price point
